title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: a tall shape in the fog: a person, or a post? you can guess either way, but only one guess is knowing
carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
tomorrow: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana as clarity: nobody thinks I am not, yet people disagree about what the self is. Did the glasses on your head turn up anywhere? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

Early morning, thick fog, a walk along a field. Up ahead, something tall stands at the edge of the path. A person, waiting? A fence post? You could decide it's a person, and your heart would speed up. You could decide it's a post and keep walking. You could even stand there and change your mind three times. None of that changes what is standing in the fog. When you get close enough, the thing itself settles the question. Shankara uses this very kind of example, a post that might be a man, while commenting on the Brahma Sutra's second line. Today: what it means that knowing depends on the thing.
screen: `A SHAPE IN THE FOG.` → `PERSON, OR POST?` → `THE THING SETTLES IT.`

segments.voice: The second line says Brahman is that from which the birth and the rest of this world come. Shankara stops here to ask a sharp question. If that's a description of a cause, couldn't we just reason our way to it? See a world, infer a maker, done. His answer is no, not on its own. The line, he says, isn't offering a stand-alone argument. It gathers the Upanishads' own sayings, and reasoning is welcome only as their helper, because Brahman is not something the senses can show you. Then comes the part about the post. When it comes to action, he says, a person has choices. You can do a ritual, skip it, or do it another way. Duty depends on the one who does it. Knowing isn't like that. Of one post in the fog, you can think post, or man, or something else, but only one of those thoughts is knowledge. The others are just opinions. Knowledge depends on the thing. And since Brahman is something that already is, not something to be done, knowing it depends on Brahman, not on our choosing. That's why, he says, this knowledge doesn't end in words alone. It is meant to culminate in direct experience. So jnana, in Shankara's hands, is the opposite of a mood or a preference. It's the moment the fog thins and the question settles itself. Not every school draws the line between doing and knowing where he does. Ramanuja, for one, joins knowing to loving meditation. Shankara draws it here, firmly.
screen: `NOT A STAND-ALONE ARGUMENT.` · `DOING HAS CHOICES.` · `KNOWING DEPENDS ON THE THING.` · `MEANT TO END IN EXPERIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something be what it is. Settle, and let your eyes rest on one plain object near you, a cup, a door handle, the edge of a table. Notice the opinions that rise about it: nice, ugly, needs cleaning. Let them go by like fog. Come back to the object itself, its shape, its color, just as it is, before you decide anything. Each time an opinion comes, notice it, and return. If you pray, you can offer this attention as it is. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, knowing that depends on the thing itself, not on our choosing, and that is meant to end in direct experience. Today's word.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. Today, before you settle an argument, ask: is this a choice, or a post in the fog? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

fork.setup: in the fog you see a tall shape. you'd rather it were a post, not a stranger. can you make it a post by deciding?
options: yes, if you decide firmly enough.
no, the thing itself settles it.
it's whatever most people say it is.
fork.reveal: Shankara's point exactly: action depends on the doer, but knowledge depends on the thing.

original.note: Sanskrit: direct experience; Shankara says knowing Brahman is meant to culminate in it.

notes: Paraphrase of Shankara on 1.1.2: the sutra is not inference alone but strings Vedanta texts together, with reasoning admitted as an aid; the contrast of action (may be done, not done, done otherwise; depends on the person) with knowledge of an existing thing (depends on the thing); the post/man example; knowledge of Brahman culminates in experience (anubhava). Confirm each detail and that the post example sits in 1.1.2.
'Ramanuja, for one, joins knowing to loving meditation' is a brief summary of his view that the knowledge enjoined is meditation of the nature of devotion. Confirm the phrasing.
